claim: The Hippo pathway has been shown to impact early development and tumorigenesis by governing cell proliferation and apoptosis.
source: The evolutionarily conserved Hippo (Hpo) pathway has been shown to impact early development and tumorigenesis by governing cell proliferation and apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about the Hippo pathway's role in development and cancer.

claim: Loss of wts-1/LATS resulted in premature deformation of touch neurons in a yap-1/YAP-dependent manner.
source: Loss of wts-1/LATS, the core kinase of the Hpo pathway, resulted in premature deformation of touch neurons and impaired touch responses in a yap-1/YAP-dependent manner, the downstream transcriptional co-activator of LATS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing neuronal deformation in wts-1 mutants that is rescued by yap-1 mutation.

claim: Decreased movement alleviated the neuronal deformation of wts-1 mutants.
source: Decreased movement as well as microtubule destabilization by treatment with colchicine or disruption of microtubule-stabilizing genes alleviated the neuronal deformation of wts-1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that RNAi knockdown of muscle machinery genes reduced neuronal defects.

claim: Colchicine treatment alleviated neuronal deformation of wts-1 mutants.
source: Decreased movement as well as microtubule destabilization by treatment with colchicine or disruption of microtubule-stabilizing genes alleviated the neuronal deformation of wts-1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced neuronal lesions in colchicine-treated wts-1 mutants.

claim: Colchicine exerted neuroprotective effects during normal aging.
source: Colchicine exerted neuroprotective effects even during normal aging.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that colchicine treatment reduced age-associated neuronal deformation in wild-type animals.

claim: Deficiency of spas-1, a microtubule-severing enzyme, led to precocious structural deformation.
source: In addition, the deficiency of a microtubule-severing enzyme spas-1 also led to precocious structural deformation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing premature neuronal deformation in spas-1 mutants.

claim: Hyper-stabilized microtubules in wts-1-deficient neurons are detrimental to the maintenance of neuronal structural integrity.
source: These results consistently suggest that hyper-stabilized microtubules in both wts-1-deficient neurons and normally aged neurons are detrimental to the maintenance of neuronal structural integrity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple experimental observations including colchicine rescue, electron microscopy, and genetic interactions.

claim: Hyper-stabilized microtubules in normally aged neurons are detrimental to the maintenance of neuronal structural integrity.
source: These results consistently suggest that hyper-stabilized microtubules in both wts-1-deficient neurons and normally aged neurons are detrimental to the maintenance of neuronal structural integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that colchicine treatment protects against age-associated neuronal deformation.

claim: The Hippo pathway governs the structural and functional maintenance of differentiated neurons by modulating microtubule stability.
source: In summary, Hpo pathway governs the structural and functional maintenance of differentiated neurons by modulating microtubule stability, raising the possibility that the microtubule stability of fully developed neurons could be a promising target to delay neuronal aging.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neurons extend their axons and dendrites from 1 μm to more than 1 m.
source: For this to happen, neuronal cells extend their axons and dendrites from 1 μm to more than 1 m and must maintain an intact morphology throughout their lifetime.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuronal anatomy.

claim: Structural abnormalities and functional decline are hallmarks of aged neurons or pathological neurons affected by neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Structural abnormalities and the consequent functional decline are hallmarks of aged neurons or pathological neurons affected by neurodegenerative diseases (Yankner et al., 2008; Bishop et al., 2010; Fjell and Walhovd, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The aged brain exhibits structural abnormalities such as synaptic loss, neuronal sprouting and restructuring, rather than neuronal cell death.
source: Several studies have shown that the aged brain exhibits structural abnormalities such as synaptic loss, neuronal sprouting and restructuring, rather than neuronal cell death (reviewed in Yankner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Microtubules serve as structural struts that allow the neuron to develop and maintain a specific shape.
source: In neurons, they serve as structural struts that allow the neuron to develop and maintain a specific shape (Barnes and Polleux, 2009; Marin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microtubules act as railroads for motor proteins that deliver cellular cargo from cell bodies to distal axons.
source: They also act as railroads for motor proteins that deliver cellular cargo from cell bodies to distal axons (Hirokawa et al., 2010; Maday et al., 2014), as well as seeds for microtubule polymerization (Job et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both hyper-stabilized or unstable microtubules are harmful for maintaining neuronal morphology.
source: Numerous studies have suggested that both hyper- or unstable microtubules are harmful for maintaining neuronal morphology as the imbalance in microtubule dynamics contributes to neurological diseases (reviewed in Dubey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Microtubule regulators have been implicated in a number of human diseases.
source: Thus, microtubule regulators have been implicated in a number of human diseases (Dubey et al., 2015; Matamoros and Baas, 2016) and signaling pathways including Notch pathway have been proposed as pharmaceutical targets for cytoskeletal protection of postnatal neurons (Bonini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: C. elegans neurons share fundamental characteristics with mammalian neurons in terms of their molecular basis and functions.
source: The neurons of Caenorhabditis elegans provide a valuable model system because they share fundamental characteristics with mammalian neurons in terms of their molecular basis and functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans as a model system.

claim: Major genetic pathways governing early neuronal development were initially identified from studies on C. elegans.
source: Major genetic pathways governing early neuronal development such as neuronal cell migration or polarization were initially identified from numerous studies on C. elegans (Hedgecock et al., 1990; Wadsworth et al., 1996; Culotti and Merz, 1998; Ikegami et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: C. elegans neurons demonstrate age-associated structural and functional deterioration.
source: Additionally, C. elegans neurons could be utilized to understand the molecular mechanism of neuronal aging as they demonstrate age-associated structural and functional deterioration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans aging.

claim: Touch receptor neurons show the most prominent decline in structure and function with aging in C. elegans.
source: In particular, touch receptor neurons (TRNs), comprising two ALM, AVM, two PLM, and PVM, show the most prominent decline in structure and function with aging (Pan et al., 2011; Tank et al., 2011; Toth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In aged C. elegans, TRNs have highly wavy or ectopically branched processes, misshaped cell bodies with abnormal morphology or outgrown processes.
source: In aged animals, TRNs have highly wavy or ectopically branched processes, misshaped cell bodies with abnormal morphology or outgrown processes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing aged TRN phenotypes.

claim: C. elegans exhibits gradual decreases in touch responses as they age.
source: Moreover, C. elegans exhibits gradual decreases in touch responses as they age (Tank et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: DAF-2/IGF pathway, JNK/MAPK pathway, and membrane activity of TRNs influence the speed of touch neuronal aging.
source: DAF-2/IGF pathway, JNK/MAPK pathway, and membrane activity of TRNs have been identified to influence the speed of touch neuronal aging by modulating whole organismal senescence or cell-autonomous functions (Pan et al., 2011; Tank et al., 2011; Toth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Hippo kinase signaling pathway is evolutionarily conserved across animal species.
source: The Hippo (Hpo) kinase signaling pathway, which is evolutionarily conserved across animal species, plays a pivotal role in the regulation of tissue size homeostasis (Harvey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The Hippo pathway regulates cell proliferation and apoptosis during early development and tumorigenesis.
source: It regulates cell proliferation and apoptosis during early development and tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway.

claim: When the Hippo pathway is active, LATS phosphorylates and inhibits the nuclear localization of YAP.
source: When the Hpo pathway is active, LATS, the core kinase of the pathway, phosphorylates and inhibits the nuclear localization of YAP, a transcriptional co-activator.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular mechanism of the Hippo pathway.

claim: In the nucleus, YAP regulates target gene expression through interaction with the TEAD transcription factor.
source: In the nucleus, YAP regulates target gene expression through interaction with the TEAD transcription factor (Zhao et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of the Hippo pathway promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation, leading to tumorigenesis and developmental problems.
source: The dysregulation of this pathway promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation, leading to tumorigenesis and developmental problems (Huang et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2007; Harvey et al., 2013; Zheng and Pan, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Core components and their genetic interaction of the Hippo pathway are conserved in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, core components and their genetic interaction of the Hpo pathway are conserved.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the C. elegans Hippo pathway.

claim: Inhibition of YAP-1/YAP by upstream WTS-1/LATS is needed for the maintenance of apicobasal membrane polarity of the developing intestine in C. elegans.
source: Inhibition of YAP-1/YAP by upstream WTS-1/LATS is needed for the maintenance of apicobasal membrane polarity of the developing intestine (Kang et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of wts-1 leads to early larval death.
source: A previous study demonstrated that the intestinal Hpo pathway is essential for the proper development of the intestinal lumen and loss of wts-1, the core kinase of the pathway, leads to early larval death (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The wts-1 mutants showed distinctive abnormalities in the morphology of TRNs.
source: We observed that the wts-1 mutants showed extremely distinctive abnormalities in the morphology of TRNs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In wild-type C. elegans, ALM and PLM extended their neuronal processes along the anterior–posterior axis and maintained structural integrity during adolescence.
source: In the wild-type, ALM and its posterior homolog PLM extended their neuronal processes along the anterior–posterior axis and maintained structural integrity during adolescence (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The wts-1 mutant ALM and PLM exhibited ectopic swelling/waviness and branching.
source: However, the wts-1 mutant- ALM and PLM exhibited ectopic swelling/waviness and branching (Figure 1A and B), and other various deformations, including extended or shortened distal processes or outgrowth of processes from the cell body (somatic outgrowth) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data shown in Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Atypical structures of AVM and PVM were found in the wts-1 mutants.
source: Atypical structures of other TRNs, AVM and PVM, were also found in the mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), indicating that wts-1 is essential in mechanosensory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: wts-1 is essential in mechanosensory neurons.
source: Atypical structures of other TRNs, AVM and PVM, were also found in the mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), indicating that wts-1 is essential in mechanosensory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple types of mechanosensory neurons show defects in wts-1 mutants.

claim: ALM and PLM complete their development during embryogenesis in C. elegans.
source: ALM and PLM complete their development during embryogenesis, whereas AVM and PVM develop until the first larval stage (L1) (Chalfie et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: AVM and PVM develop until the first larval stage (L1) in C. elegans.
source: ALM and PLM complete their development during embryogenesis, whereas AVM and PVM develop until the first larval stage (L1) (Chalfie et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The wts-1 mutant had intact, unaltered neuronal processes of ALM and PLM at the very early L1 stage.
source: The wts-1 mutant had intact, unaltered neuronal processes of ALM and PLM at the very early L1 stage and the frequency of abnormal neurons gradually increased as the worms grew (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The frequency of abnormal neurons in wts-1 mutants gradually increased as the worms grew.
source: The wts-1 mutant had intact, unaltered neuronal processes of ALM and PLM at the very early L1 stage and the frequency of abnormal neurons gradually increased as the worms grew (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At the L4 stage, 98.89% of ALM and 84.44% of PLM showed at least one morphological abnormality in the wts-1 mutant.
source: At the fourth larval (L4) stage, 98.89% of ALM and 84.44% of PLM, respectively, showed at least one morphological abnormality in the mutant, whereas they maintain intact structures in the wild-type (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ectopic swelling and branching on the processes were the most common abnormalities in wts-1 mutant TRNs.
source: Among the abnormalities, ectopic swelling and branching on the processes were the most common (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F), followed by extension of the distal process and somatic outgrowth of the cell body (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: The number of ectopic swelling/branching increased as the worms grew in wts-1 mutants.
source: Ectopic swelling or branching occurred in multiple places in a single process and the number of swelling/branching also increased as the worms grew (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Dopaminergic, GABAergic, and cholinergic neurons maintained structures comparable with those of the wild-type in wts-1 mutants.
source: Dopaminergic, GABAergic, and cholinergic neurons were found to maintain structures comparable with those of the wild-type at the same age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and K.

claim: ALN, a cholinergic neuron that extends its process in association with ALM, preserved structural integrity in wts-1 mutants.
source: It is noteworthy that ALN, a cholinergic neuron that extends its process in association with ALM (White et al., 1986), preserved their structural integrity in the mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Loss of wts-1 leads to structural deformities specifically in TRNs.
source: Thus, we concluded that the loss of wts-1 leads to a wide range of structural deformities specifically in TRNs and that this deformity is a matter of maintenance, rather than development of the structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only TRNs show defects while other neuron types remain intact.

claim: The deformity in wts-1 mutant TRNs is a matter of maintenance, rather than development of the structures.
source: Thus, we concluded that the loss of wts-1 leads to a wide range of structural deformities specifically in TRNs and that this deformity is a matter of maintenance, rather than development of the structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TRNs develop normally but degenerate over time in wts-1 mutants.

claim: TRNs govern the aversive movements of worms in response to gentle body touches.
source: TRNs govern the aversive movements of worms in response to gentle body touches (Chalfie et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: At the L4 stage, control worms responded to almost every gentle touch (9.40 responses/10 touches), whereas wts-1 mutants responded to 60% of stimuli (6.31/10).
source: At the L4 stage, control worms responded to almost every gentle touch (9.40 responses/10 touches), whereas wts-1 mutants responded to 60% of stimuli (6.31/10) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: On the first day of adulthood (1DA), control worms showed slightly decreased touch responses compared with the L4 stage (8.25/10), whereas wts-1 mutants displayed more impaired responses (5.57/10).
source: On the first day of adulthood (1DA), control worms showed slightly decreased touch responses compared with the L4 stage (8.25/10), whereas wts-1 mutants displayed more impaired responses (5.57/10) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The structural and functional decline in the wts-1 mutants is similar to the phenotypes of normally aged animals.
source: The structural and functional decline in the wts-1 mutants is very similar to the phenotypes of normally aged animals.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of wts-1 mutant phenotypes with previously described aging phenotypes.

claim: Aging of human brain in the absence of disease is often accompanied by structural deformation, such as dendritic restructuring, neuronal sprouting, and synaptic losses, rather than severe neuronal degeneration or cell death.
source: Aging of human brain in the absence of disease is often accompanied by structural deformation, such as dendritic restructuring, neuronal sprouting, and synaptic losses, rather than severe neuronal degeneration or cell death (Yankner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Structural abnormalities of ALM or PLM appear from the 4th day of adulthood and occur in almost every individual after the 15th day of adulthood in C. elegans.
source: Structural abnormalities of ALM or PLM appear from the 4th day of adulthood and occur in almost every individual after the 15th day of adulthood (Toth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The degree of morphological deformation of the L4 stage wts-1 was similar to that of the aged wild-type worms on the 15th day of adulthood.
source: According to our observations, the degree of morphological deformation of the L4 stage wts-1 was similar to that of the aged wild-type worms on the 15th day of adulthood.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental observations.

claim: Loss of wts-1 leads to structural and functional impairment of TRNs precociously.
source: These results suggest that loss of wts-1 leads to structural and functional impairment of TRNs precociously.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that wts-1 mutants show aging-like phenotypes at young ages.

claim: The wts-1; yap-1 mutant displayed intact neuronal processes without any swelling or branching.
source: In contrast to the wts-1 mosaic mutant, the wts-1; yap-1 mutant could survive without intestinal WTS-1 expression as previously reported (Lee et al., 2019) and displayed intact neuronal processes without any swelling or branching (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Introduction of a mutation in egl-44 was sufficient to suppress the structural abnormalities of wts-1 TRNs.
source: Introduction of a mutation in egl-44, which is the worm homolog of TEAD and functions downstream of wts-1 along with yap-1 in the developing intestine (Lee et al., 2019), was also sufficient to suppress the structural abnormalities of wts-1 TRNs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: TRNs in the wts-1 mutant properly innervate the epidermal layer.
source: Initially, we observed TRNs of the wts-1 mutant properly innervate the epidermal layer (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) comparable to the wild-type (Emtage et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TRNs in the wts-1 mutant showed differences in both the number and morphology of microtubules compared to the wild-type.
source: However, TRNs in the wts-1 mutant showed differences in both the number and morphology of microtubules compared to the wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy observations.

claim: In wild-type TRNs, multiple microtubules with characteristic spherical shapes were observed.
source: In wild-type TRNs, multiple microtubules with characteristic spherical shapes were observed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the wts-1 mutant ALM, the number of microtubules significantly decreased.
source: In contrast, in the wts-1 mutant ALM, the number of microtubules significantly decreased (n = 16, 4, 18, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and the morphology was also irregular and non-spherical (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The morphology of microtubules in wts-1 mutant ALM was irregular and non-spherical.
source: In contrast, in the wts-1 mutant ALM, the number of microtubules significantly decreased (n = 16, 4, 18, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and the morphology was also irregular and non-spherical (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The abnormalities in the number and shape of microtubules of TRNs were restored in the wts-1; yap-1 mutant.
source: Consistent with our finding using a fluorescence marker, the abnormalities in the number and shape of microtubules of TRNs were restored in the wts-1; yap-1 mutant (n = 24, 30, 44, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The loss of yap-1 restored the impaired touch responses of the wts-1 mutant.
source: The loss of yap-1 also restored the impaired touch responses of the wts-1 mutant. In comparison with the wts-1 mutant, touch responses of the wts-1; yap-1 double mutant were significantly rescued (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The wts-1 mutant had a shorter lifespan than the wild-type.
source: The wts-1 mutant had a shorter lifespan than the wild-type, suggesting that prematurely deformed neurons of the wts-1 mutant were probably due to accelerated organismal aging (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The wts-1; yap-1 mutant had a slightly shorter lifespan than the wts-1 mutant.
source: However, given that the wts-1; yap-1 mutant with restored neurons had a slightly shorter lifespan than the wts-1 mutant (Figure 2F) and only TRNs were affected in the mutant, premature deformation of the wts-1 neurons appeared to be a touch neuron-specific event, rather than being associated with whole body.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Premature deformation of the wts-1 neurons is a touch neuron-specific event, rather than being associated with whole body aging.
source: However, given that the wts-1; yap-1 mutant with restored neurons had a slightly shorter lifespan than the wts-1 mutant (Figure 2F) and only TRNs were affected in the mutant, premature deformation of the wts-1 neurons appeared to be a touch neuron-specific event, rather than being associated with whole body.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neuronal rescue does not extend lifespan and only TRNs are affected.

claim: TRNs-specific knockdown of wts-1 induced significant disintegration of TRNs such as ectopic neuronal swelling or shortened neuronal process.
source: While the control did not have any abnormalities of TRNs, every transgenic lines showed significant disintegration of TRNs such as ectopic neuronal swelling or shortened neuronal process as seen in wts-1 mutant at L4 stage (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: WTS-1 functions in TRNs to maintain intact neuronal structures.
source: These results documented that WTS-1 functions in TRNs to maintain intact neuronal structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TRN-specific knockdown of wts-1 causes neuronal defects.

claim: Touch neuronal expression of YAP-1 was sufficient to re-emerge ectopic neuronal swelling in the wts-1; yap-1 mutants.
source: Touch neuronal expression of YAP-1 using a mec-4 promoter was sufficient to re-emerge ectopic neuronal swelling in the wts-1; yap-1 mutants. Approximately 40% of transgenic worms exhibited ectopic swelling and branching on ALM or PLM. In contrast, siblings containing no transgene preserved intact neuronal processes (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Overexpression of YAP is commonly observed in many human cancers and is associated with poor prognosis of the diseases.
source: Overexpression of YAP is commonly observed in many human cancers and is associated with poor prognosis of the diseases (Liu et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inducible overexpression of YAP is sufficient to increase liver size in mice through transcriptional regulation of downstream genes that activate cell proliferation.
source: Inducible overexpression of YAP is sufficient to increase liver size in mice through transcriptional regulation of downstream genes that activate cell proliferation (Dong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpressing YAP-1 in TRNs causes multiple neuronal defects in a dose-dependent manner.
source: To see if TRNs-specific overexpression of YAP-1 is sufficient to induce neuronal abnormalities, we overexpressed Pmec-4::YAP-1 in a wild-type and found that overexpressing YAP-1 causes multiple neuronal defects in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 3G-J.

claim: wts-1 and yap-1 act in a cell-autonomous manner to induce structural disintegration of TRNs.
source: These results demonstrated that wts-1 and yap-1 act in a cell-autonomous manner to induce structural disintegration of TRNs; thus, proper regulation of YAP-1 activity by WTS-1 is important to maintain neuronal structural integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific rescue and knockdown experiments.

claim: Proper regulation of YAP-1 activity by WTS-1 is important to maintain neuronal structural integrity.
source: These results demonstrated that wts-1 and yap-1 act in a cell-autonomous manner to induce structural disintegration of TRNs; thus, proper regulation of YAP-1 activity by WTS-1 is important to maintain neuronal structural integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction studies showing that YAP-1 activity must be controlled by WTS-1.

claim: Neuronal processes contain bundles of microtubules, which are essential structural foundations that protect neurons from mechanical strain-induced damage.
source: Neuronal processes contain bundles of microtubules, which are essential structural foundations that protect neurons from mechanical strain-induced damage (Tang-Schomer et al., 2010; Krieg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of unc-54 severely impaired organismal movement.
source: As previously reported (MacLeod et al., 1977; Neumann and Hilliard, 2014), the knockdown of muscle machinery genes, including a myosin heavy chain gene (unc-54), severely impaired organismal movement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous literature.

claim: unc-54 RNAi resulted in a significant reduction in neuronal swelling/branching events in ALM as well as PLM in wts-1 mutants.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, unc-54 RNAi resulted in a significant reduction in neuronal swelling/branching events in ALM as well as PLM (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: The control ALM showed 7.67 lesions on average, whereas ALM treated with unc-54 RNAi had 4.851 lesions at the L4 stage.
source: The control ALM showed 7.67 lesions on average, whereas ALM treated with unc-54 RNAi had 4.851 lesions at the L4 stage.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from the experiments.

claim: For PLM, the events of swelling/branching occurred 6.59 times on average in the controls, whereas 2.96 in the unc-54 RNAi-fed neurons at the L4 stage.
source: For PLM, the events of swelling/branching occurred 6.59 times on average in the controls, whereas 2.96 in the unc-54 RNAi-fed neurons at the same stage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The knockdown of unc-15 or unc-95 showed movement defects and exhibited ameliorative effects on neuronal structures in wts-1 mutants.
source: The knockdown of unc-15 or unc-95, which encodes paramyosin (a structural component of thick filaments) and muscle LIM domain protein, respectively (Kagawa et al., 1989; Broday et al., 2004), showed movement defects as well and exhibited ameliorative effects on neuronal structures (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The severity of movement defects is inversely correlated with the severity of neuronal deformation in wts-1 mutants.
source: These observations indicate that the severity of movement defects is inversely correlated with the severity of neuronal deformation, and it strongly supports the hypothesis that wts-1 neurons are vulnerable to physical stresses generated by organismal movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between movement impairment and neuronal protection.

claim: wts-1 neurons are vulnerable to physical stresses generated by organismal movements.
source: These observations indicate that the severity of movement defects is inversely correlated with the severity of neuronal deformation, and it strongly supports the hypothesis that wts-1 neurons are vulnerable to physical stresses generated by organismal movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that reducing movement protects wts-1 neurons.

claim: Colchicine greatly reduced the morphological abnormalities of the wts-1 mutant neurons.
source: Interestingly, colchicine, a microtubule-destabilizing agent (Vandecandelaere et al., 1997), greatly reduced the morphological abnormalities of the wts-1 mutant neurons (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 4G-K.

claim: The drug-untreated ALM showed 5.88 swelling/branching events on a process, whereas the colchicine-treated ALM only had 2.95 swelling/branching.
source: The drug-untreated ALM showed 5.88 swelling/branching events on a process, whereas the colchicine-treated ALM only had 2.95 swelling/branching.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from the experiments.

claim: In the case of PLM, colchicine treatment reduced neuronal lesions from 4.41 to 0.89.
source: In the case of PLM, colchicine treatment reduced neuronal lesions from 4.41 to 0.89 (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Treatment with colchicine significantly improved touch responses of the wts-1 mutants at L4 stage.
source: Furthermore, treatment with colchicine significantly improved touch responses of the mutants at L4 stage (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Treatment with paclitaxel failed to mitigate neuronal abnormalities of the wts-1 mutants.
source: In contrast, treatment with paclitaxel, a microtubule-stabilizing agent (Schiff et al., 1979; Vandecandelaere et al., 1997; Yvon et al., 1999), failed to mitigate neuronal abnormalities of the wts-1 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Treatment with colchicine, not paclitaxel, lessened the morphological and functional alteration of wts-1 neurons.
source: These results show that treatment with colchicine, not paclitaxel, lessened the morphological and functional alteration of wts-1 neurons, suggesting that hyper-stabilized microtubules are responsible for the structural and subsequent functional decline of the mutant neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of microtubule-destabilizing vs. stabilizing drugs.

claim: Hyper-stabilized microtubules are responsible for the structural and functional decline of wts-1 mutant neurons.
source: These results show that treatment with colchicine, not paclitaxel, lessened the morphological and functional alteration of wts-1 neurons, suggesting that hyper-stabilized microtubules are responsible for the structural and subsequent functional decline of the mutant neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that destabilizing microtubules rescues the phenotype while stabilizing them does not.

claim: Both ALM and PLM of colchicine-treated worms maintained intact structures even after 20 days of adulthood (20DA).
source: Notably, both ALM and PLM of colchicine-treated worms maintained intact structures even after 20 days of adulthood (20DA) (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: While untreated 20DA had approximately 73.1% and 57.5% defective ALM and PLM, respectively, colchicine-treated worms showed only 23.6% and 7.2% defective ALM and PLM, respectively.
source: While untreated 20DA had approximately 73.1% and 57.5% defective ALM and PLM, respectively, colchicine-treated worms showed only 23.6% and 7.2% defective ALM and PLM, respectively (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Colchicine treatment significantly reduced multiple structural abnormalities of TRNs, including somatic outgrowth of ALM and ectopic swelling or branching of PLM.
source: Colchicine treatment significantly reduced multiple structural abnormalities of TRNs, including somatic outgrowth of ALM and ectopic swelling or branching of PLM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: Colchicine treatment improved touch responses of aged animals.
source: More importantly, colchicine treatment also improved touch responses of aged animals. Whereas there was no difference between touch responses of colchicine-treated and untreated 2DA animals, drug-treated 10DA animals showed significantly higher touch responses compared to the untreated controls (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Colchicine treatment did not affect worm lifespan.
source: Considering that the same method of colchicine treatment did not affect worm lifespan (Figure 5F), the protective effects of colchicine on the structural and functional integrity of TRNs are unlikely to be derived from the prolonged lifespan of worms.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The protective effects of colchicine on the structural and functional integrity of TRNs are unlikely to be derived from the prolonged lifespan of worms.
source: Considering that the same method of colchicine treatment did not affect worm lifespan (Figure 5F), the protective effects of colchicine on the structural and functional integrity of TRNs are unlikely to be derived from the prolonged lifespan of worms.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that colchicine protects neurons without extending lifespan.

claim: Treatment with paclitaxel significantly increased neuronal defects of ALM in aged animals.
source: We found that colchicine treatment not only rescued structural defects of spas-1 mutant, but also increased touch responses of the mutant at 2DA (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: Hyper-stabilized microtubules could be responsible for age-related neuronal degeneration.
source: Taken together, hyper-stabilized microtubules could be responsible for age-related neuronal degeneration, and neuronal status of the wts-1 mutant was similar to that of aged neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both colchicine and paclitaxel have consistent effects on aging and wts-1 phenotypes.

claim: Neuronal status of the wts-1 mutant was similar to that of aged neurons.
source: Taken together, hyper-stabilized microtubules could be responsible for age-related neuronal degeneration, and neuronal status of the wts-1 mutant was similar to that of aged neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar responses to drug treatments and similar phenotypes.

claim: Spastin is an ATP-dependent microtubule-severing enzyme.
source: Spastin, an ATP-dependent microtubule-severing enzyme, is known to cause a human neurodegenerative disease, hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) (Hazan et al., 1999; Svenson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hyper-stabilized microtubules by the loss of spastin activity have been considered as a main contributor of HSP disease pathology.
source: Hyper-stabilized microtubules by the loss of spastin activity have been considered as a main contributor of disease pathology (Sherwood et al., 2004; Evans et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SPAS-1 possesses a microtubule-severing activity and is expressed in the TRNs.
source: SPAS-1, the worm homolog of spastin, possesses a microtubule-severing activity and is expressed in the TRNs (Matsushita Ishiodori et al., 2007; Brown and El Bejjani, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The spas-1 mutants exhibit premature deformation of TRNs.
source: We found that the spas-1 mutants exhibit premature deformation of TRNs. From the second day of adulthood (2DA), the mutant ALM displayed an accelerated onset of neuronal deformity (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: Expression of SPAS-1 under mec-4 promoter restored premature deformation of the spas-1 mutant ALM.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, expression of SPAS-1 under mec-4 promoter, as well as spas-1 own promoter, restored premature deformation of the spas-1 mutant ALM (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Human SPAST expression under the control of the C. elegans spas-1 promoter displayed rescue effects on spas-1 mutant ALM.
source: Human SPAST expression under the control of the C. elegans spas-1 promoter displayed similar rescue effects, whereas the loss-of-function mutant (K388R), which is associated with disease pathology (Fonknechten et al., 2000), failed to restore the structural integrity of the mutant ALM (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The loss-of-function mutant SPAST(K388R) failed to restore the structural integrity of the spas-1 mutant ALM.
source: Human SPAST expression under the control of the C. elegans spas-1 promoter displayed similar rescue effects, whereas the loss-of-function mutant (K388R), which is associated with disease pathology (Fonknechten et al., 2000), failed to restore the structural integrity of the mutant ALM (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Colchicine treatment rescued structural defects of spas-1 mutant.
source: We found that colchicine treatment not only rescued structural defects of spas-1 mutant, but also increased touch responses of the mutant at 2DA (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Colchicine treatment increased touch responses of the spas-1 mutant at 2DA.
source: We found that colchicine treatment not only rescued structural defects of spas-1 mutant, but also increased touch responses of the mutant at 2DA (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: In human spastin, K388R mutation completely abrogates the ATP binding in the ATPase region and microtubule-severing activity.
source: In human spastin, K388R mutation completely abrogates the ATP binding in the ATPase region and microtubule-severing activity (Evans et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Microtubule-severing activity of SPAST is likely conserved in C. elegans SPAS-1.
source: Taken together, microtubule-severing activity of SPAST is likely conserved in C. elegans SPAS-1, and it is important to protect neuronal structures from gradual deformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with human SPAST and the failure of the K388R mutant to rescue.

claim: The loss of microtubule-severing enzyme led to accelerated neuronal deformation, supporting that hyper-stabilized microtubules are responsible for the age-associated structural decline of neurons.
source: Moreover, the fact that the loss of microtubule-severing enzyme led to accelerated neuronal deformation also supports that hyper-stabilized microtubules are responsible for the age-associated structural decline of neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of spas-1 causes premature neuronal aging.

claim: Loss of microtubule-stabilizing genes dlk-1 and ptl-1 delayed premature deformation of wts-1 neurons.
source: Both wts-1; dlk-1 and wts-1; ptl-1 displayed improved TRNs structures. The total number of ectopic lesions was significantly reduced, and the proportion of intact neurons without any deformed structures was also highly increased (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: The loss of microtubule-stabilizing genes mitigates the structural deformation of the wts-1, supporting that the wts-1 mutants have highly stabilized microtubules which are responsible for the structural deformation.
source: The fact that the loss of microtubule-stabilizing genes mitigates the structural deformation of the wts-1 also supports the finding that the wts-1 mutants have highly stabilized microtubules which are responsible for the structural deformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction studies showing that reducing microtubule stability rescues wts-1 phenotypes.

claim: ptl-1 encodes the sole C. elegans homolog of the microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT).
source: ptl-1 encodes the sole C. elegans homolog of the microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) (McDermott et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In mammals, tau is predominantly localized to the neuronal axons and promotes microtubule assembly and stability.
source: In mammals, tau is predominantly localized to the neuronal axons and promotes microtubule assembly and stability; moreover, mutations in the MAPT locus are highly associated with several neurodegenerative diseases, such as FTD-17 (Goedert and Spillantini, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mutations in the MAPT locus are highly associated with several neurodegenerative diseases, such as FTD-17.
source: In mammals, tau is predominantly localized to the neuronal axons and promotes microtubule assembly and stability; moreover, mutations in the MAPT locus are highly associated with several neurodegenerative diseases, such as FTD-17 (Goedert and Spillantini, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The loss of ptl-1 results in premature structural disintegration of TRNs in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, the loss of ptl-1 itself results in premature structural disintegration of TRNs (Chew et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The structural decline seen in the ptl-1 mutants is probably due to microtubule destabilization, unlike those observed in the wts-1 mutants.
source: Given these observations with the wts-1; ptl-1 mutants and the revealed functions of MAPT, the structural decline seen in the ptl-1 mutants is probably due to the microtubule destabilization, unlike those observed in the wts-1 mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of tau/PTL-1 in stabilizing microtubules.

claim: The loss of yap-1 increased the structural abnormalities of ptl-1 mutants.
source: Consistent with this assumption, the loss of yap-1 did not lessen structural deformation of ptl-1, even increased the structural abnormalities of ptl-1 (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Loss of yap-1 could probably lead to microtubule destabilization.
source: Loss of yap-1 could probably lead to microtubule destabilization and has a redundant effect on microtubule stability with microtubule destabilization due to ptl-1 loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that yap-1 loss worsens ptl-1 phenotypes.

claim: Loss of wts-1 results in postnatal deformation of TRNs.
source: In this study, we showed that the loss of wts-1, the core kinase of the Hpo pathway, results in postnatal deformation of TRNs.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The features of defective TRNs in the wts-1 mutant closely resemble those of aged TRNs.
source: The detailed observation of morphological alteration in wts-1 mutant suggests that the features of defective TRNs in the wts-1 mutant closely resemble those of aged TRNs (Toth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with previously described aging phenotypes.

claim: Both yap-1 and egl-44 act as downstream of wts-1 in TRN maintenance.
source: We also defined that both yap-1 and egl-44 act as downstream of wts-1 and that TRNs-specific rescue of YAP-1 was sufficient to re-induce the neuronal deformation of wts-1; yap-1 double mutant.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction studies.

claim: The Hippo pathway of C. elegans has a neuroprotective effect in differentiated neurons in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: These observations say that the Hpo pathway of C. elegans has a neuroprotective effect in differentiated neurons in a cell-autonomous manner, restricting YAP-1 from triggering premature neuronal decline.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tissue-specific rescue and knockdown experiments.

claim: Dysregulation of the Hippo pathway has been implicated in aging and pathologies of the nervous system.
source: In addition to its extensively studied roles in early development and tumorigenesis, dysregulation of the Hpo pathway has been implicated in aging and pathologies of the nervous system (Sahu and Mondal, 2020; Gogia et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hyper-activation of MST1 and the consequent inhibition of YAP have been noted in several neurodegenerative disease models.
source: Hyper-activation of the pathway components such as MST1 and the consequent inhibition of YAP have been noted in several neurodegenerative disease models (Matsumoto et al., 2014; Yamanishi et al., 2017; Mueller et al., 2018; Tanaka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In neurodegenerative disease models, the inactivation of the Hippo pathway or the activation of YAP ameliorates neuronal cell death.
source: In these models, the inactivation of the pathway or the activation of YAP ameliorates neuronal cell death; thus, the manipulation of the Hpo pathway has been regarded to prevent pathologies associated with neuronal cell death.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of the Hippo pathway and ectopic activation of YAP have been observed in patients with Alexander disease.
source: Moreover, some examples present the detrimental effects of uncontrolled YAP. Dysregulation of the pathway and ectopic activation of YAP have been observed in patients with Alexander disease, which is a rare neurodegenerative disease that results in progressive neuronal degeneration based on the loss of myelin (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The activation of YAP occurred in Müller cells during retinal degeneration.
source: Further, the activation of YAP also occurred in Müller cells during retinal degeneration (Hamon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Proper regulation of YAP is essential to maintain neuronal integrity.
source: The present study shows that proper regulation of YAP is essential to maintain neuronal integrity and adds important information to the research on anti-aging roles of the Hpo pathway after development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Defective, hyper-stabilized microtubules in the wts-1 mutant were responsible for premature deformation of neurons, possibly in a 'wear-to-tear fashion' because of the mechanical strains generated by organismal movements.
source: Genetic and pharmacological approaches suggest that defective, hyper-stabilized microtubules in the wts-1 mutant were responsible for premature deformation of neurons, possibly in a 'wear-to-tear fashion' because of the mechanical strains generated by organismal movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of movement reduction, drug treatment, and genetic studies.

claim: Colchicine binds irreversibly to tubulin dimers and prevents the addition of tubulin dimers to the fast-growing ends of microtubule.
source: Colchicine binds irreversibly to tubulin dimers and prevents the addition of tubulin dimers to the fast-growing ends of microtubule (Ravelli et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Colchicine has been widely used to cure acute gouty arthritis and familial Mediterranean fever (FMF).
source: It has been widely used to cure acute gouty arthritis and familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) (Dinarello et al., 1974; Zemer et al., 1974; Zemer et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Colchicine treatment on fully developed animals largely reduced age-related failures in neuronal structures and functions during normal aging.
source: Moreover, colchicine treatment on fully developed animals largely reduced age-related failures in neuronal structures and functions during normal aging.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing protection of aged neurons by colchicine.

claim: Hyper-stabilization of neuronal microtubules would be a promising target to cure age-associated neuronal deformation.
source: This supports the idea that neuronal deformation seen in the wts-1 mutants is similar to that in aged organism, and, more importantly, hyper-stabilization of neuronal microtubules would be a promising target to cure age-associated neuronal deformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing colchicine's protective effects.

claim: Microtubule-destabilizing agents mimic several neuronal degenerative disease phenotypes.
source: These observations are unexpected because microtubule-destabilizing agents mimic several neuronal degenerative disease phenotypes, and microtubule-stabilizing agents such as paclitaxel and epothilone D exhibit neuroprotective effects in the pathological contexts (Zhang et al., 2005; Shemesh and Spira, 2011; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microtubule-stabilizing agents such as paclitaxel and epothilone D exhibit neuroprotective effects in pathological contexts.
source: These observations are unexpected because microtubule-destabilizing agents mimic several neuronal degenerative disease phenotypes, and microtubule-stabilizing agents such as paclitaxel and epothilone D exhibit neuroprotective effects in the pathological contexts (Zhang et al., 2005; Shemesh and Spira, 2011; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Colchicine has detrimental effects on cognitive function in animal disease models specifically leading to cholinergic neuronal loss.
source: Some reports have shown that colchicine has detrimental effects on cognitive function in animal disease models specifically leading to cholinergic neuronal loss (Goldschmidt and Steward, 1982; Veerendra Kumar and Gupta, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Long-term colchicine treatment could protect against cognitive decline in older patients with FMF.
source: In contrast, a study in older patients with FMF showed that long-term colchicine treatment could protect against cognitive decline in patients (Leibovitz et al., 2006) and the neuroprotective functions of colchicine also have been reported (Pratt et al., 1994; Salama et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In HSP and paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy, hyper-stabilization of microtubule could be a cause of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: In the case of HSP and paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy, hyper-stabilization of microtubule could be a cause of neurodegenerative diseases (Cavaletti et al., 1995; Hazan et al., 1999; Trotta et al., 2004; Evans et al., 2005; Lee and Swain, 2006; Scripture et al., 2006; Gornstein and Schwarz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutated spastin is the most common cause of HSP, a hereditary, neurodegenerative disease that affects the upper motor neurons.
source: Mutated spastin is the most common cause of HSP, a hereditary, neurodegenerative disease that affects the upper motor neurons (Hazan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Vinblastine, a microtubule-destabilizing agent, rescues axonal swellings in the HSP models.
source: Similar to the neuroprotective effects of colchicine in the wts-1 or aged neurons, vinblastine, a microtubule-destabilizing agent, rescues axonal swellings in the HSP models (Fassier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Impaired spastin activity in several animal models results in sparser microtubule array at axons.
source: Additionally, the fact that impaired spastin activity in several animal models results in sparser microtubule array at axons (Sherwood et al., 2004; Wood et al., 2006) provides a possible link between hyper-stabilization and the sparseness of microtubules we observed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Shared properties among wts-1 mutant neurons, aged neurons, and HSP models strongly support that the hyper-stabilized microtubules are responsible for the structural and functional failures of neurons in both senescent and pathological conditions.
source: These shared properties among wts-1 mutant neurons, aged neurons, and HSP models strongly support that the hyper-stabilized microtubules are responsible for the structural and functional failures of neurons in both senescent and pathological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of multiple experimental systems.

claim: Mutations in several tubulin proteins, microtubule-binding proteins such as tau, and failures in nerve attachment to the epidermis have been reported to induce similar deformities in TRNs.
source: Mutations in several tubulin proteins, microtubule-binding proteins such as tau, and failures in nerve attachment to the epidermis have been reported to induce similar deformities in TRNs, as seen in the wts-1 mutant.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from previous literature.

claim: In several mutants of mec-1, TRNs fail to separate from body-wall muscles and they are prematurely degenerated.
source: In several mutants of mec-1, which encodes an ECM protein, TRNs fail to separate from body-wall muscles and they are prematurely degenerated (Pan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TRNs of the wts-1 mutant appeared to normally dissociate from the muscles and innervate the epidermal layer.
source: In contrast to the mec-1 mutant neurons, TRNs of the wts-1 mutant appeared to normally dissociate from the muscles and innervate the epidermal layer.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy observations.

claim: The phenotype of the wts-1 mutant appears much earlier, and its phenotypic penetrance is notably higher compared with any other known mutant.
source: Despite these limitations in understanding the underlying mechanism, the phenotype of the wts-1 mutant appears much earlier, and its phenotypic penetrance is notably higher compared with any other known mutant.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously described mutants.

claim: Defective TRNs of the wts-1 mutant could provide a neuronal model to investigate the potential therapeutic targets for improving neuronal aging.
source: As we have shown in this study, defective TRNs of the wts-1 mutant could provide a neuronal model to investigate the potential therapeutic targets for improving neuronal aging that occurs either prematurely or normally.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential utility of the model.
